title: Give each brand its own currency contract

blocks.text: The merchant's contracts differ by brand. Visa purchases may be in euro (978), US dollars (840) or pounds (826). Mastercard purchases may only be in euro, and the acquirer wants those refusals answered with 57 rather than the usual 58. Last quarter a property name misspelt in a descriptor left a check like this one switched off for a week, and nobody noticed.

`AcceptedCurrencies` in `src/main/java/com/example/practice/AcceptedCurrencies.java` sits in both brand groups of the TransactionManager, configured differently in each. Finish `setConfiguration` and `prepare`, marked `TODO`. The comment at the top of the class lists the properties. About a dozen lines in total.

The tests deploy a real TransactionManager with Q2, in the test's own JVM, with `SelectDestination`, `Switch` and a `visa` and a `mastercard` group. They send purchases of both brands in several currencies.

cases.says: a purchase in a currency both contracts cover goes on to be approved, for either brand
a purchase in a currency its brand's contract doesn't cover is declined with that group's code, and the terminal gets the answer
two participant elements of one class keep their own configuration, so each brand applies its own list and code
a missing or misspelt currencies property is refused at configuration time instead of meaning an empty list

origin.section: 5.4 Each `<participant>` Element Is Its Own Instance, With Its Own Configuration

concepts: Each participant element is its own instance with its own configuration; static configuration lets the last element configured decide for all.
A missing or misspelt required property is refused in setConfiguration, so the deploy fails instead of the check passing everything.
